new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is lexically contrastive (penult vs final minimal pairs such as lábat 'cold' / labát 'cross-eyed', áddu 'many' / addú 'two'); its position is not predictable and is written with an acute on every form. Primary stress is realised as vowel length (in open syllables) plus higher pitch. Suffixes -an / -uhn usually pull stress onto themselves, but a lexical class of roots keeps its stress.
new_statements.secondary_stress: A secondary stress may occur, always before the primary; it is marked by length only (same pitch as unstressed syllables). It arises e.g. when a root retains its own stress before a stressed suffix (túbug-án type vs tubugán); no secondary stress when stress simply shifts from a root-final vowel to the suffix; not written on closed syllables because closed syllables are all long and the contrast is inaudible there.
new_statements.exceptions: Some variation in placement in context: kótye 'car' but kotyé ku 'my car', atawá but atawa kú, versus báka / báka ku, wagí / wagí ku with no shift; roots like sírib, tappét, túyat, tulát keep stress under -an/-uhn suffixation while most roots (bantúl, tubúg) shift it to the suffix; accent placement can signal number (ának 'children' vs anák); u~o free variation irrelevant to stress.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level lexical stress; authors state the 'basic' stress of a root is that of the unaffixed form with determiners yu/tu; the dictionary site notes the language 'does not resort to prosodics beyond the word'. Phrase-level: enclitic pronouns can attract or host the accent (atawa kú).
new_statements.identity_note: Both Davis sources describe the Yogad of Echague, Isabela (data from one principal speaker, Dr. Angel Mesa, life-long Echague resident); this is the language-level languoid yoga1237 with no dialect split in Glottolog. The author's open PDFs (philipwdavis.com) are dated 1997 (grammar) and 1999 (dictionary, 4th printing) and correspond to the Lincom print editions of 1998 and 2000; grammar pagination differs by about one page from print, dictionary roman-numeral pagination matches Google Books hits.

sources.note: Fullest account (pp. xvii-xxiv): lexical stress is distinctive (minimal pairs lábat/labát, páyaw/payáw, áddu/addú, kúku/kukú, ámma/ammá, áttit/attít, taláttak/talatták); primary stress = greater length (open syll.) + higher pitch; a secondary stress may precede the primary (length only, no pitch); suffixes -an/-uhn usually attract stress, some roots keep it; 'position of stress remains highly variable in Yogad'; stress written where heard; some variation in context (kótye ~ kotyé ku).

sources.note: Print p.5-6 (author PDF p.6): 'Lexical stress is distinctive and is noted with an accute accent. Examples of this contrast are: lábat cold / labát cross-eyed; páyaw / payáw; áddu many / addú two; kúku / kukú; ámma father / ammá if, when. There is some variation in the placement of accent in context, and we try to write it where we hear it' (kótye ~ kotyé ku, atawá ~ atawa kú, but báka ku, wagí ku). p.3: all vowels longer in open syllables when stressed. p.22 fn: ának (pl.) vs anák shows accent placement signalling number. Ch.6 (p.266): -uhn suffix and stress position.
